questions.question: The Modern Period (1914–1945) in English literary history is bracketed by the outbreak of World War I in 1914 and the end of:
options: The Crimean War in Eastern Europe
The Boer War in South Africa
questions.explanation: The Modern Period spans from the start of the First World War in 1914 to the conclusion of the Second World War in 1945.

questions.question: Which year is celebrated as the 'annus mirabilis' of High Modernism for the publication of both 'Ulysses' and 'The Waste Land'?
questions.explanation: In 1922 James Joyce published 'Ulysses' in Paris and T. S. Eliot published 'The Waste Land', making 1922 the pinnacle of High Modernism.

questions.question: Which modernist narrative technique, used by James Joyce and Virginia Woolf, records the continuous flow of a character's inner thoughts?
questions.explanation: Stream of consciousness renders the Associative, uninterrupted flow of perceptions and memories inside a character's mind.

questions.question: Which First World War poet wrote 'Dulce et Decorum Est', 'Anthem for Doomed Youth', and 'Strange Meeting' before dying in action in 1918?
questions.explanation: Wilfred Owen wrote the most celebrated anti-war trench poems of World War I and was killed on 4 November 1918, one week before the Armistice.

questions.question: Which World War I officer and poet mentored Wilfred Owen at Craiglockhart Hospital and wrote 'Counter-Attack' (1918)?
questions.explanation: Siegfried Sassoon encouraged Wilfred Owen at Craiglockhart War Hospital in 1917 and published Owen's 'Poems' in 1920.

questions.question: Which British soldier-poet and painter wrote 'Break of Day in the Trenches' and 'Dead Man's Dump' before being killed in April 1918?
questions.explanation: Britannica highlights Isaac Rosenberg as one of the most original World War I poets; he was killed in action in April 1918.

questions.question: Which poet and novelist published the disillusioned World War I autobiography 'Good-Bye to All That' in 1929?
questions.explanation: Robert Graves published his candid war memoir 'Good-Bye to All That' in 1929 and later wrote the Roman novels 'I, Claudius' and 'Claudius the God'.

questions.question: Which poet and dramatist became the first Irish writer to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923?
questions.explanation: W. B. Yeats received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923 for his inspired poetry giving expression to the spirit of a whole nation.

questions.question: In W. B. Yeats's poem 'Easter, 1916', commemorating the Irish rebellion against British rule, what famous refrain is repeated?
options: 'That is no country for old men'
'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold'
questions.explanation: Yeats's 'Easter, 1916', collected in 'Michael Robartes and the Dancer' in 1921, repeats the refrain A terrible beauty is born.

questions.question: Which apocalyptic poem by W. B. Yeats (written 1919) contains the famous line 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold'?
questions.explanation: Yeats's 'The Second Coming' uses the image of a widening gyre and a rough beast slouching towards Bethlehem.

questions.question: Which 1928 poetry collection by W. B. Yeats—named after his Norman castle in Galway—opens with 'Sailing to Byzantium'?
questions.explanation: Yeats's 1928 volume 'The Tower' is one of his supreme modernist collections, opening with 'Sailing to Byzantium'.

questions.question: Which 1915 poem by T. S. Eliot begins 'Let us go then, you and I, / When the evening is spread out against the sky'?
options: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock'
questions.explanation: Eliot published 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' in 'Poetry' magazine in 1915 and in 'Prufrock and Other Observations' in 1917.

questions.question: Which landmark 1922 modernist poem by T. S. Eliot opens with the line 'April is the cruellest month'?
questions.explanation: T. S. Eliot's five-part poem 'The Waste Land' of 1922 opens Section I, 'The Burial of the Dead', with April is the cruellest month.

questions.question: To which fellow poet—calling him 'il miglior fabbro' ('the better craftsman')—did T. S. Eliot dedicate 'The Waste Land' (1922)?
questions.explanation: Ezra Pound heavily edited the manuscript of 'The Waste Land', and Eliot dedicated the poem to him using Dante's phrase for Arnaut Daniel.

questions.question: Which 1935 verse drama by T. S. Eliot portrays the 1170 assassination of Archbishop Thomas Becket at Canterbury?
questions.explanation: Eliot wrote 'Murder in the Cathedral' in 1935 for the Canterbury Festival, dramatizing Becket's martyrdom.

questions.question: What is the title of T. S. Eliot's meditative sequence (published together in 1943) comprising 'Burnt Norton', 'East Coker', 'The Dry Salvages', and 'Little Gidding'?
questions.explanation: Eliot composed 'Four Quartets' between 1935 and 1942 and published the complete four-poem volume in 1943.

questions.question: Which 1920 critical volume by T. S. Eliot contains his famous essay 'Tradition and the Individual Talent'?
options: 'The Use of Poetry and the Use of Criticism'
questions.explanation: Eliot's first book of literary criticism, 'The Sacred Wood: Essays on Poetry and Criticism', appeared in 1920.

questions.question: In James Joyce's 1916 bildungsroman 'A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man', who is the autobiographical protagonist?
questions.explanation: Stephen Dedalus, named after Saint Stephen and the mythical artificer Daedalus, is the hero of 'A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man'.

questions.question: James Joyce's modernist novel 'Ulysses' (1922) takes place in Dublin over the course of which single day, celebrated as 'Bloomsday'?
questions.explanation: All eighteen episodes of Joyce's 'Ulysses' unfold on a single day, 16 June 1904, the date of Joyce's first outing with Nora Barnacle.

questions.question: Which experimental 1939 novel was James Joyce's final work, written over seventeen years in a polyglot dream-language of puns?
questions.explanation: Serialized in fragments as 'Work in Progress', Joyce's 'Finnegans Wake' was published in May 1939.

questions.question: Which publishing house was founded by Leonard and Virginia Woolf in 1917 and published T. S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land' in book form in Britain?
questions.explanation: Leonard and Virginia Woolf established the Hogarth Press in 1917 at Hogarth House, Richmond.

questions.question: Which 1925 novel by Virginia Woolf follows a London society hostess preparing for a party on a single June day alongside war veteran Septimus Warren Smith?
questions.explanation: Woolf's 1925 novel 'Mrs. Dalloway' interweaves Clarissa Dalloway's party preparations with the shell-shocked Septimus Warren Smith.

questions.question: Which 1927 novel by Virginia Woolf portrays Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay and the painter Lily Briscoe at their summer home in the Hebrides?
questions.explanation: Woolf's 1927 elegiac novel 'To the Lighthouse' is structured in three parts: 'The Window', 'Time Passes', and 'The Lighthouse'.

questions.question: Which 1928 novel by Virginia Woolf—dedicated to Vita Sackville-West—follows an Elizabethan poet who lives for three centuries and becomes a woman?
questions.explanation: Woolf published 'Orlando: A Biography' in 1928 as a playful fantasy of literary history and gender identity inspired by Vita Sackville-West.

questions.question: In which 1929 feminist treatise did Virginia Woolf declare that 'a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction'?
questions.explanation: Based on lectures at Newnham and Girton Colleges, Cambridge, Woolf's 'A Room of One's Own' appeared in 1929.

questions.question: Which two connected novels by D. H. Lawrence (1915 and 1920) follow the Brangwen family and the sisters Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen?
questions.explanation: Lawrence traced the generational history of the Brangwens in 'The Rainbow' in 1915 and its sequel 'Women in Love' in 1920.

questions.question: Which 1928 novel by D. H. Lawrence, privately printed in Florence and long banned in Britain, depicts Constance Chatterley and the gamekeeper Mellors?
questions.explanation: Lawrence's final novel, 'Lady Chatterley's Lover', was printed in Florence in 1928 and remained banned in Britain until the 1960 trial.

questions.question: Which 1915 modernist novel by Ford Madox Ford opens 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard' and uses the unreliable narrator John Dowell?
questions.explanation: Ford Madox Ford's 'The Good Soldier: A Tale of Passion' of 1915 is a classic of modernist unreliable narration.

questions.question: What is the title of Ford Madox Ford's four-novel sequence (1924–1928) about Christopher Tietjens and the First World War?
questions.explanation: Ford's 'Parade's End' tetralogy comprises 'Some Do Not...', 'No More Parades', 'A Man Could Stand Up—', and 'Last Post'.

questions.question: Which 1924 novel by E. M. Forster examines racial tension and colonial rule in British India through Dr. Aziz, Cyril Fielding, and Adela Quested?
questions.explanation: Forster's 'A Passage to India' of 1924 centres on Adela Quested's accusation against Dr. Aziz after visiting the Marabar Caves.

questions.question: In which 1927 work of literary criticism did E. M. Forster introduce the distinction between 'flat' and 'round' characters?
questions.explanation: Forster delivered the Clark Lectures at Trinity College, Cambridge, and published them in 1927 as 'Aspects of the Novel'.

questions.question: Which New Zealand-born modernist writer gained acclaim for short-story collections such as 'Bliss' (1920) and 'The Garden Party' (1922)?
questions.explanation: Katherine Mansfield revolutionized the English modernist short story with Chekhovian subtlety in 'Bliss' and 'The Garden Party'.

questions.question: Which British writer began her thirteen-volume stream-of-consciousness novel sequence 'Pilgrimage' with 'Pointed Roofs' in 1915?
questions.explanation: Dorothy Richardson published 'Pointed Roofs' in 1915 as the first volume of 'Pilgrimage', following Miriam Henderson's consciousness.

questions.question: Which 1932 dystopian novel by Aldous Huxley depicts a futuristic World State where citizens are conditioned in hatcheries and pacified with 'soma'?
questions.explanation: Aldous Huxley published 'Brave New World' in 1932, portraying a technocratic dystopia dated in the year of Our Ford 632.

questions.question: From which play by William Shakespeare—spoken by Miranda—did Aldous Huxley borrow the title 'Brave New World' (1932)?
questions.explanation: In Act V of Shakespeare's 'The Tempest', Miranda exclaims O brave new world, That has such people in't!

questions.question: Which four left-wing poets of the 1930s were collectively dubbed 'MacSpaunday' by satirist Roy Campbell?
options: Wilfred Owen, Siegfried Sassoon, Robert Graves, and Edmund Blunden
Louis MacNeice, Stephen Spender, W. H. Auden, and Cecil Day-Lewis
Dylan Thomas, Philip Larkin, Ted Hughes, and Seamus Heaney
Hugh MacDiarmid, Ezra Pound, T. S. Eliot, and William Butler Yeats
questions.explanation: Roy Campbell coined the composite name MacSpaunday in 'Talking Bronco' for MacNeice, Spender, Auden, and Day-Lewis.

questions.question: Which leading poet of the 1930s generation wrote 'Spain' (1937), 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats' (1939), and 'September 1, 1939'?
questions.explanation: Wystan Hugh Auden was the central figure of the 1930s poets, authoring 'Spain', 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats', and 'September 1, 1939'.

questions.question: Under which pen name did Eric Arthur Blair (1903–1950) publish 'The Road to Wigan Pier' (1937), 'Homage to Catalonia' (1938), and 'Animal Farm' (1945)?
questions.explanation: Eric Arthur Blair adopted the pen name George Orwell with the publication of 'Down and Out in Paris and London' in 1933.

questions.question: Which satirical beast fable by George Orwell, published in August 1945, allegorizes the Russian Revolution and Stalinism through the pigs Napoleon and Snowball?
questions.explanation: Orwell's 'Animal Farm: A Fairy Story' was published on 17 August 1945, satirizing Soviet totalitarianism.

questions.question: George Orwell's 1938 personal account 'Homage to Catalonia' records his experience fighting in a militia during which 1936–1939 conflict?
questions.explanation: Orwell fought with the POUM militia in the Spanish Civil War and was wounded in the throat by a sniper, as told in 'Homage to Catalonia'.

questions.question: Which satirical novelist wrote 'Decline and Fall' (1928), 'A Handful of Dust' (1934), and 'Brideshead Revisited' (1945)?
questions.explanation: Evelyn Waugh satirized the Bright Young Things of the 1920s and published 'Brideshead Revisited' in 1945.

questions.question: Which Catholic novelist authored the thriller-morality novels 'Brighton Rock' (1938) and 'The Power and the Glory' (1940)?
questions.explanation: Graham Greene merged thriller plots with Catholic moral ambiguity in 'Brighton Rock' in 1938 and 'The Power and the Glory' in 1940.

questions.question: Who authored the 1939 Berlin stories volume 'Goodbye to Berlin', featuring the cabaret character Sally Bowles as Nazism rises in Germany?
questions.explanation: Christopher Isherwood published 'Mr Norris Changes Trains' in 1935 and 'Goodbye to Berlin' in 1939, declaring I am a camera.

questions.question: Which Irish playwright wrote the 'Dublin Trilogy'—'The Shadow of a Gunman' (1923), 'Juno and the Paycock' (1924), and 'The Plough and the Stars' (1926)?
questions.explanation: Sean O'Casey portrayed working-class Dubliners during the Irish revolutionary period in his three Abbey Theatre masterpieces of 1923–1926.

questions.question: Which English dramatist achieved interwar West End acclaim with witty comedies such as 'Hay Fever' (1925), 'Private Lives' (1930), and 'Blithe Spirit' (1941)?
questions.explanation: Noël Coward broke through with 'The Vortex' in 1924 and became the master of interwar sophisticated comedy.

questions.question: Which 1923 history play about the Maid of Orleans helped earn George Bernard Shaw the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.explanation: Shaw's 'Saint Joan', premiered in 1923 and published in 1924 after Joan of Arc's 1920 canonization, is widely regarded as his greatest tragedy.

questions.question: Which Cambridge theorist laid the foundations of New Criticism and 'close reading' in 'Principles of Literary Criticism' (1924) and 'Practical Criticism' (1929)?
questions.explanation: I. A. Richards pioneered close reading by having Cambridge students analyze unsigned poems in 'Practical Criticism' in 1929.

questions.question: Which student of I. A. Richards published the influential 1930 critical study 'Seven Types of Ambiguity'?
questions.explanation: William Empson wrote 'Seven Types of Ambiguity' in 1930 at age 24, demonstrating the multiple meanings generated by poetic language.

questions.question: Which influential Cambridge critic co-founded and edited the quarterly review 'Scrutiny' from 1932 to 1953?
questions.explanation: F. R. Leavis edited 'Scrutiny' from 1932 to 1953 and published 'New Bearings in English Poetry' in 1932.

questions.question: Which Welsh poet rose to fame with '18 Poems' (1934) and the autobiographical stories 'Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog' (1940)?
questions.explanation: Dylan Thomas brought neo-romantic lyrical intensity back to British poetry in the 1930s and 1940s.
